verb.modalVerbsDoNot: Modal verbs do not change with the subject (he can, never “cans”), have no to-infinitive or -ing form, and are always followed by the bare infinitive without “to”.

verb.ukBritishUsageUs: UK = British usage, US = American usage. The tables below follow the variety you choose.
verb.irregularVerbLearnV2: Irregular verb: learn V2 and V3 by heart. The -ing and -s forms still follow the normal rules.
verb.justAddEdIng: Just add -ed, -ing or -s – no spelling change.
verb.subject: Subject
verb.almostNeverUsedIn: Almost never used in real English.
verb.thePassiveIsRare: The passive is rare in this tense – use another tense instead.
verb.stativeVerbUsuallyNot: Stative verb: usually not used in continuous tenses (I know, not I am knowing).
verb.continuousFormsAreFine: Continuous forms are fine for an action meaning (I’m thinking about it), but not for an opinion or state (I think so).
verb.theNegativeOfMust: The negative of “must have” (deduction) is can’t have / couldn’t have; it is rarely used in questions.

verb.experiencesPresentResultsAndThings: Experiences, present results, and things that have just happened.

verb.finishedActionsAtASpecific: Finished actions at a specific time in the past.

verb.anActionThatHappenedBefore: An action that happened before another past action.
verb.aProcessThatContinuedUp: A process that continued up to a point in the past.
verb.existingPlansAndPredictionsBased: Existing plans and predictions based on evidence.
verb.actionsInProgressAtAMoment: Actions in progress at a moment in the future.
verb.actionsThatWillBeFinished: Actions that will be finished before a point in the future.
verb.aProcessThatWillContinue: A process that will continue up to a point in the future.
verb.theFutureSeenFromThe: The future seen from the past (reported speech).
verb.aPastPlanThatOften: A past plan (that often did not happen).
verb.regretOrCriticismTheRight: Regret or criticism: the right thing was not done.
verb.aPastPossibilityThatDid: A past possibility that did not happen.
verb.anUncertainGuessAboutThe: An uncertain guess about the past.
verb.aPossibleGuessAboutThe: A possible guess about the past.
verb.anAlmostCertainConclusionAbout: An almost certain conclusion about the past.
verb.ifAVerbEndsIn: If a verb ends in consonant + vowel + consonant and the last syllable is stressed, double the final consonant (stop → stopped, begin → beginning).
verb.britishEnglishDoublesTheFinal: British English doubles the final -l (travelled); American English does not (traveled).
verb.consonantYChangeYTo: Consonant + y: change y to i, then add -ed/-es (studied, studies). Vowel + y keeps the y (played).
verb.dropTheSilentEBefore: Drop the silent -e before -ing, and add only -d for -ed (making, loved).
verb.verbsEndingInEeOe: Verbs ending in -ee, -oe or -ye keep the -e before -ing (agreeing, canoeing).
verb.addKAfterIcBefore: Add k after -ic before -ed/-ing to keep the /k/ sound (panicked, panicking).
verb.addEsAfterSX: Add -es after s, x, z, ch, sh and consonant + o (watches, goes).
verb.theFinalSoundIsT: The final sound is /t/ or /d/ → add an extra syllable /ɪd/.
verb.theFinalSoundIsVoiceless: The final sound is voiceless (/p k f s ʃ tʃ θ/) → say /t/.
verb.theFinalSoundIsA: The final sound is a vowel or voiced (/b g v z m n l r/…) → say /d/.
verb.afterAHissingSoundS: After a hissing sound /s z ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ/ → add an extra syllable /ɪz/.
verb.afterAVoicelessSoundP: After a voiceless sound /p t k f θ/ → say /s/.
verb.afterAVowelOrVoiced: After a vowel or voiced sound → say /z/.
verb.afterDidDidnTUse: After did / didn’t, use the base form.
verb.afterHaveHasHadUse: After have / has / had, use the past participle (V3), not V2.
verb.afterDoesDoesnTThe: After does / doesn’t, the verb takes no -s.
verb.stativeVerbsAreUsuallyNot: Stative verbs are usually not used in continuous tenses.
verb.spellingMistakeSeeTheSpelling: Spelling mistake – see the spelling rules above.
verb.agreeIsAVerbDo: “agree” is a verb – do not use it with am/is/are.
verb.thisVerbIsFollowedBy: This verb is followed by -ing, not by to + verb.
verb.arriveInACityOr: arrive in (a city or country) / arrive at (a place) – never “arrive to”.
verb.lieRestFlatLayLain: lie (rest flat) – lay – lain has no object; lay (put down) – laid – laid needs an object.
verb.riseGoUpByItself: rise (go up by itself) has no object; raise (lift or increase something) needs an object.
verb.beBornIsAFixed: “be born” is a fixed form: I was born.
verb.beActsAsItsOwn: “be” acts as its own auxiliary – it never uses do / does / did.
verb.lookForwardToIngTo: look forward to + -ing (“to” is a preposition here).
verb.suggestRecommendThatSubjectVerb: suggest / recommend + that + subject + verb (or + -ing), not “someone to + verb”.
verb.neverUseTwoModalVerbs: Never use two modal verbs together: say “will be able to”.
verb.lendGiveForATime: lend = give for a time; borrow = take for a time.
verb.tellAPersonSaySomething: tell + a person; say + something (say to someone).
verb.britishEnglishUsesHaveGot: British English uses “have got”; “gotten” is American English.
verb.afterAModalVerbUse: After a modal verb, use the base form with no -s.
verb.modalVerbsMoveToThe: Modal verbs move to the front in questions – no “do”.

skill.qt.trueBaiNoiDung: TRUE: the passage says the same thing (often in different words). FALSE: the passage says the opposite. NOT GIVEN: the passage does not give enough information to decide. Watch qualifiers such as all, some, only, always, and do not use outside knowledge. Answers follow the order of the passage.
skill.qt.cauHoiVeQuan: These questions ask about the writer's views, not general facts. YES: the writer agrees; NO: the writer disagrees; NOT GIVEN: the writer gives no opinion on it. Look for attitude words (argue, claim, unfortunately…). Answers follow the order of the passage.
skill.qt.gachChanTuKhoa: Underline the key words in the question before you read or listen. An option that repeats the exact words of the text is often a trap; the correct answer is usually paraphrased. In Listening, speakers often mention several options – choose the one that is finally confirmed.
skill.qt.chonDu2Dap: Choose exactly 2 answers (order does not matter; each correct answer scores 1 mark). Read all 5 options carefully and rule out any option that is mentioned but denied, or that belongs to a different person or thing.
skill.qt.docDanhSachTieu: Read the list of headings first, then read the first and last sentences of each paragraph. The right heading sums up the main idea of the whole paragraph, not just one detail; be wary of headings that repeat exact words from the text. Do the easy paragraphs first to narrow the choices – there are always more headings than paragraphs.
skill.qt.dapAnKhongTheo: Answers are not in passage order, and a paragraph may be used more than once. Decide what kind of information you need (an example, a reason, a figure, a comparison…) and then scan. Do this task after the other tasks on the same passage, when you already know the content.
skill.qt.timVaDanhDau: Find and mark the names (people, organisations, dates) in the passage first, then read closely around each name and compare it with the paraphrased statement. Answers are not in passage order; an option may be used more than once or not at all.
skill.qt.docPhanDauCau: Read the sentence beginning and predict what the missing part needs (in meaning and grammar). The correct ending must fit both the grammar and the content of the passage. Questions follow the order of the passage; there are always more endings than questions.
skill.qt.truocKhiNgheXac: Before you listen, find the starting point, the directions (north/south, left/right) and the places already labelled. Listen for position words: opposite, next to, behind, at the end of, turn left… Follow each step of the route on the map; answers come in the order of the recording.
skill.qt.docDanhSachLua: Read the list of options first and think of synonyms. Speakers often mention several options for each item – wait for the one that is finally confirmed. Items come in the order of the recording; some options are not used.
skill.qt.dungThoiGianTruoc: Use the time before the recording to read the questions and predict the type of information needed (a name, number, date, price…). Speakers often correct themselves (“…no, sorry, it’s 15”) – write the final information. Spell correctly and stay within the word limit; answers follow the order of the recording.
skill.qt.tieuDeGhiChu: The title of the notes or table tells you which part of the passage to read; answers usually come in order. Predict the word type for each gap, copy the word exactly from the passage (do not change its form) and stay within the word limit.
skill.qt.docLuotCaDoan: Skim the whole summary to find which part of the passage it covers, then predict the word type for each gap. If you choose words from a box, the answer is usually a synonym rather than the exact word in the passage. After filling the gaps, check the grammar (singular/plural).
skill.qt.docCaCauVa: Read the whole sentence and predict the type of word needed (noun, number, adjective…). Copy the word exactly from the passage, spell it correctly and stay within the word limit; the completed sentence must be grammatical. Answers usually follow the order of the passage.
skill.qt.nhinAnhTruocKhi: Look at the photo before you listen: who is there, what they are doing, which objects you see and where. Rule out statements that mention things not in the photo or use similar-sounding words. Distinguish between “is being + V3” (an action in progress – someone must be doing it) and “has been + V3” (a finished state).
skill.qt.ngheThatKyTu: Listen very carefully to the question word at the start (Who, When, Where, Why, How…). Rule out answers that repeat words or use words that sound like the question. Indirect answers (“Let me check”, “Ask Mr. Kim”) are often correct; Wh- questions are not answered with Yes/No.
skill.qt.docTruoc3Cau: Read the 3 questions (and any graphic) while the directions are being read. Questions usually follow the conversation: topic/place → details → what happens next. The correct answer is usually a paraphrase of what is said.
skill.qt.docTruocCauHoi: Read the questions first. The first question often asks about the purpose or the audience – the answer comes in the opening sentences. Listen for requests, suggestions and schedule changes near the end of the talk.
skill.qt.nhin4PhuongAn: Look at the 4 options first: different word forms (noun/verb/adjective/adverb) → check the position of the gap; different tenses → look for time markers and the subject; different meanings → read the whole sentence. Many questions need only 20–30 seconds – save time for Part 7.
skill.qt.giongPart5Nhung: Like Part 5, but you must read the sentences before and after the gap, especially for linking words, verb tenses and pronouns. For sentence-insertion gaps, choose the sentence that connects with both the sentence before and the sentence after.
skill.qt.docCauHoiTruoc: Read the questions first, then scan the text for key words. In multiple-passage sets, some questions require combining information from 2 texts. “NOT true” questions and sentence-insertion questions take longer – you can leave them for later. Aim for about 1 minute per question.
skill.qt.docCaCauDe: Read the whole sentence to work out the word (word type, meaning), then fill in the missing letters with correct spelling. Watch grammatical endings: plural -s, past -ed, adverb -ly. Do the easy words quickly first.
skill.qt.xacDinhLoaiVan: Identify the type of text (notice, email, text message, advertisement) and its purpose. Questions are mostly about practical details: times, places and what the reader needs to do – scan for numbers, dates and names.
skill.qt.docCauChuDe: Read the topic sentence of each paragraph to get the main idea, then find details for each question. Inference questions: choose what the passage implies, not an option that just repeats words. Vocabulary questions: put each option into the sentence and check that the meaning stays the same.
skill.qt.nhanRaLoaiCau: Identify the type of remark (asking for information, a suggestion, an invitation, a complaint) and choose the most natural reply. Rule out replies that repeat the speaker's words but do not answer the point.
skill.qt.theoDoiVanDe: Follow the speaker's problem and the solution or action they decide on. Take short notes: who, what they need, what happens next.
skill.qt.namMucDichThong: Get the purpose of the announcement (a change, a reminder, an event) and what listeners must do (deadline, place, how to sign up).
skill.qt.ghiChuTheoCau: Take notes in a structure: main topic → supporting points → examples. Questions usually ask about the main idea, key details and why the lecturer mentions an example.
skill.qt.xacDinhChuNgu: Find the subject and main verb first, then place the auxiliary or question word, then the remaining chunks. Indirect questions keep statement word order (…where the library is).
skill.qt.traLoiDuMoi: Answer every point the task asks for, in a tone suited to the reader, with a clear opening, body and closing. Keep the last 1–2 minutes to check grammar and spelling.
skill.qt.neuRoQuanDiem: State your opinion clearly in the first sentence, give 1–2 reasons with specific examples, and refer to other people's posts to add a new idea instead of repeating theirs.
skill.qt.ngheTronCauVa: Listen to the whole sentence and remember it in meaning chunks, not word by word. Repeat it in the same order, keeping the stress and intonation; speaking clearly matters more than speaking fast.
skill.qt.traLoiThangCau: Answer the question directly in your first 1–2 sentences, then add reasons and personal examples. Speak naturally rather than reciting; if you stumble, correct yourself and keep going.

speak.pron.theDauLuoiRa: Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth and blow gently – don't keep it behind your teeth.
speak.pron.giuDauLuoiSau: Keep your tongue tip behind your top teeth – don't stick it out; hiss like a snake: “sss”.
speak.pron.chamDauLuoiVao: Touch your tongue tip to the ridge behind your top teeth, then release – don't stick your tongue out.
speak.pron.theDauLuoiGiua: Put your tongue tip between your teeth, push air out and use your voice (touch your throat to feel the buzz).
speak.pron.dauLuoiChamLoi: Tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth, then release with your voice on – no tongue between the teeth.
speak.pron.giuLuoiSauRang: Keep your tongue behind your teeth and buzz “zzz” like a bee – no tongue between the teeth.
speak.pron.amCuoiSKhong: A final /s/ has no voice and the vowel before it is short: say “rice” crisply with a clear hiss.
speak.pron.amCuoiZRung: A final /z/ is voiced and the vowel before it is longer: “riiise-zzz”.
speak.pron.dungNuotAmCuoi: Don't swallow the last sound: close and lightly release the final /t/, /k/, /p/ or /d/.
speak.pron.tuNayKetThuc: This word ends in a vowel – don't add a final consonant; just let the vowel finish naturally.
speak.pron.phuAmCuoiVo: Voiceless final sound: keep the vowel short and finish with a crisp /t/, /k/ or /f/.
speak.pron.phuAmCuoiHuu: Voiced final sound: make the vowel longer and keep your voice on for the final /d/, /ɡ/ or /v/.
speak.pron.cuoiTuPKhep: Final /p/: close your lips after a short vowel and release a little air – no voice.
speak.pron.cuoiTuBNguyen: Final /b/: make the vowel longer, close your lips and keep your voice on – don't turn it into “p”.
speak.pron.tuNayODang: This is the singular form – stop after the last sound, with no extra /s/.
speak.pron.dungBoDuoiS: Don't drop the -s: say the final /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/ clearly.
speak.pron.dayLaDangNguyen: This is the base form – end cleanly, with no extra /t/ or /d/.
speak.pron.docRoDuoiEd: Say the -ed ending clearly: /t/ after voiceless sounds, /d/ after voiced sounds, /ɪd/ after t or d.
speak.pron.chuMoiTronRa: Round your lips and push them forward, pull your tongue back a little and say “shh” /ʃ/.
speak.pron.moiDetDauLuoi: Keep your lips flat and your tongue tip near your top teeth; make a thin “sss” – no lip rounding.
speak.pron.batDauBangMot: Start with a quick /t/ stop, then release into “ch” – short and sharp.
speak.pron.khongChanLuoiDe: No stop: let the air flow continuously, “shhh”.
speak.pron.nhuChNhungKhong: Like “ch” with no voice – just a burst of air.
speak.pron.cungKhauHinhVoi: The same mouth shape as “ch” but with your voice on: the “j” in “jeep”.
speak.pron.chanLuoiRoiBat: Stop with your tongue, then release into a voiced “dʒ”, lips slightly rounded.
speak.pron.khongChanLuoiSau: No stop: tongue behind your teeth, a continuous “zzz”.
speak.pron.amJCoChan: The “j” sound has a tongue stop and voice – it is stronger than “y”.
speak.pron.amJNheLuot: The /j/ sound is soft, a quick “ee” glide – your tongue doesn't touch the roof of your mouth.
speak.pron.congDauLuoiLen: Curl your tongue tip up but do NOT touch the roof of your mouth; round your lips a little.
speak.pron.dauLuoiChamChac: Press your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth and let the air flow around the sides.
speak.pron.dauLuoiChamLoi2: Tongue tip on the ridge, but the air goes out through your mouth – not your nose.
speak.pron.dauLuoiChamLoi3: Tongue tip on the ridge and the air goes out through your nose (pinch your nose to feel the difference).

speak.pron.tuNayCoThem: This word has an extra light /ə/ syllable – say both syllables.

speak.pron.thaLongMiengDoc: Relax your mouth and keep the vowel short – between “ee” and “eh”.
speak.pron.haMiengRongHa: Open your mouth wide and drop your jaw – like “eh” moving towards “ah”.
speak.pron.miengMoVuaCam: Open your mouth only halfway and don't drop your jaw – a short “eh”.
speak.pron.miengMoVuaTha: Mouth half open and relaxed – a short “uh”.
speak.pron.haMiengThatTo: Open wide, tongue low, a long “ahh” as at the doctor's.

write.criteria.bonTieuChiCham: Four criteria are used for both Task 1 and Task 2 and weighted equally (25% each); in the Writing score, Task 2 counts twice as much as Task 1.
write.criteria.task2TraLoi: Task 2: address every part of the question, state a clear position, then develop and support your ideas. Task 1 (Task Achievement): give an overview, select and report the key features, with accurate data.
write.criteria.chiDapUngDe: Responds to the task only minimally, or the answer drifts off the point.
write.criteria.coNeuQuanDiem: A position is given but it is unclear; main ideas are hard to identify and may be repetitive, irrelevant or poorly supported.
write.criteria.docLuotDeRoi: Skimming the prompt and writing about the general topic instead of the actual question.
write.criteria.coLapTruongNhung: A position is expressed, but its development is not always clear and there may be no conclusion; main ideas are limited, not developed enough, and may include irrelevant detail.
write.criteria.deHoiHaiY: The question has two parts, but only one is answered.
write.criteria.traLoiMoiPhan: Addresses all parts of the task, though some more fully than others.
write.criteria.lapTruongPhuHop: The position is relevant, but conclusions may become unclear or repetitive; main ideas are relevant, but some are not developed enough or are unclear.
write.criteria.lietKeNhieuY: Listing many ideas without explaining why they matter or what they lead to.
write.criteria.traLoiMoiPhan2: Addresses all parts of the task with a clear position throughout.
write.criteria.yChinhDuocNeu: Main ideas are presented, extended and supported, but there may be over-generalisation or supporting ideas that lack focus.
write.criteria.danChungKieuEveryone: Sweeping claims such as "everyone knows that…" instead of specific examples.
write.criteria.traLoiDayDu: Sufficiently addresses all parts of the task.
write.criteria.baiPhatTrienTot: A well-developed response with relevant, extended and supported ideas; there may be occasional small gaps in content.
write.criteria.vietQuaDaiMot: Spending too long on one idea and running out of time for the other.
write.criteria.traLoiTronVen: Fully addresses all parts of the task.
write.criteria.lapTruongDuocPhat: A fully developed position that answers the question directly, with relevant, fully extended and well-supported ideas; lapses in content are extremely rare.
write.criteria.khongCoDiemYeu: No typical weakness at this level.
write.criteria.cachSapXepY: How logically ideas are sequenced, how paragraphs are used, and how accurately and naturally cohesive devices (linking words, reference, substitution) are used.
write.criteria.coYNhungSap: Ideas are present but not arranged coherently, with no clear progression.
write.criteria.dungVaiTuNoi: Some basic linking words are used, but they may be inaccurate or repetitive; paragraphing may be missing or confusing.
write.criteria.vietCaBaiThanh: Writing the whole essay as one block, or starting a new paragraph for every sentence.
write.criteria.coToChucNhung: There is some organisation, but the overall progression is not clear.
write.criteria.tuNoiDungThieu: Linking words are inadequate, inaccurate or over-used; weak reference and substitution lead to repetition; paragraphing may be inadequate or illogical.
write.criteria.cauNaoCungMo: Starting almost every sentence with Firstly, Secondly, Moreover…
write.criteria.yDuocSapXep: Ideas are arranged coherently, with a clear overall progression.
write.criteria.tuNoiDungKha: Linking words are used fairly effectively, but cohesion within or between sentences may be faulty or mechanical; reference is not always clear; paragraphs are used, but not always logically.
write.criteria.dungThisHoacIt: Using "this" or "it" without a clear reference.
write.criteria.yDuocSapXep2: Ideas are logically organised, with clear progression throughout.
write.criteria.dungNhieuPhuongTien: A range of cohesive devices is used flexibly, with some under- or over-use; each paragraph has a clear central topic.
write.criteria.tuNoiKhienCuong: Forced linking, such as using "Furthermore" before a contrasting point.
write.criteria.trinhTuYLogic: Ideas are sequenced logically, and all aspects of cohesion are well managed.
write.criteria.chiThinhThoangCo: There are only occasional lapses in cohesion; paragraphing is sufficient and appropriate.
write.criteria.themTuNoiChi: Adding linking words just to look academic.
write.criteria.lienKetTuNhien: Cohesion is so natural that it attracts no attention.
write.criteria.saiSotVeMach: Any lapses in coherence or cohesion are minimal; paragraphing is skilfully managed.
write.criteria.doRongVaDo: The range and accuracy of vocabulary: precise word choice and style, collocation, spelling and word formation.
write.criteria.vonTuCoBan: Basic vocabulary that may be repetitive or unsuitable for the task.

write.criteria.vonTuHanChe: Limited vocabulary, but just enough for the task.

write.criteria.vonTuDuCho: An adequate range of vocabulary for the task.

write.criteria.dungTuDaoTo: Using memorised "big words" with the wrong shade of meaning.
write.criteria.vonTuDuRong: Enough range to allow some flexibility and precision.
write.criteria.dungDuocTuIt: Uses less common words with some awareness of style and collocation, though some choices are inappropriate; only a few spelling or word-formation errors.
write.criteria.lanTuVanNoi: Mixing informal words (a lot of, kids, stuff) into an academic essay.
write.criteria.vonTuRongDung: A wide range of vocabulary, used fluently and flexibly to convey precise meaning.

write.criteria.thinhThoangMotCollocation: An occasional collocation that is not quite natural.

write.criteria.loiNhoCucHiem: Minor errors are extremely rare and occur only as slips.

write.criteria.noiTiepDuocVa: Keeps going and is willing to give long answers.

write.criteria.troiChayChiThinh: Fluent, with only very occasional repetition or self-correction.

write.criteria.thinhThoangDungDe: Occasionally pausing to find a precise word.
write.criteria.troiChayRatHiem: Fluent, with very rare repetition or self-correction.
write.criteria.ngapNgungNeuCo: Any hesitation is used to prepare content, not to find words or grammar; topics are developed fully coherently and extended appropriately.

write.criteria.duTuChoCa: Enough vocabulary for familiar and unfamiliar topics, but with limited flexibility.
write.criteria.coThuDienDat: Attempts to paraphrase, but not always successfully.
write.criteria.nhoiThanhNguHoc: Forcing memorised idioms (e.g. "raining cats and dogs") into the wrong context.
write.criteria.duTuDeNoi: Enough vocabulary to discuss topics at length.
write.criteria.doiKhiDungTu: Word choice is sometimes inappropriate, but meaning is clear; generally paraphrases successfully.

write.criteria.dungTuLinhHoat: Uses vocabulary flexibly across a variety of topics.

write.criteria.motVaiCollocationChua: A few collocations that are not quite natural.
write.criteria.vonTuRongDung2: A wide range of vocabulary, used readily and flexibly to convey precise meaning on all topics.
write.criteria.dungKheoTuIt2: Skilful use of less common and idiomatic words, despite occasional inaccuracies in word choice and collocation; paraphrases effectively when needed.
write.criteria.thinhThoangMotThanh: An occasional idiom that does not quite fit the context.
write.criteria.dungTuHoanToan: Complete flexibility and precision in all contexts.
write.criteria.dungTuChinhXac: Accurate and idiomatic language is used naturally and consistently.
write.criteria.doDaDangVa2: The range and accuracy of grammatical structures in speech.
write.criteria.noiDuocCauCo: Produces basic sentence forms; some short utterances are error-free.
write.criteria.hiemKhiDungMenh: Subordinate clauses are rare; answers are short, structures repetitive and errors frequent.
write.criteria.noiYesterdayIGo: Saying "Yesterday I go…" when talking about the past.
write.criteria.cauCoBanKha: Basic sentence forms are fairly accurate.
write.criteria.coThuCauPhuc: Complex structures are attempted but are limited in range, nearly always contain errors and may need rephrasing.

write.criteria.cauPhucThuongCo: Errors are frequent in complex structures, but they rarely block communication.
write.criteria.neCauPhucVi: Avoiding complex sentences for fear of mistakes, so answers sound flat.
write.criteria.dungLinhHoatNhieu: A range of structures is used flexibly; error-free sentences are frequent.
write.criteria.cauDonVaCau: Both simple and complex sentences are used effectively despite some errors; a few basic errors remain.

write.criteria.cauTrucDaDang3: A wide range of structures, used flexibly; most sentences are error-free.

write.criteria.cauTrucChinhXac: Structures are precise and accurate at all times.
write.criteria.chiCoNhungSo: The only slips are the kind native speakers also make in natural speech.

write.criteria.tuVungDonGian: Simple vocabulary (very useful, good camera, take photo, search information), with few natural expressions.

write.criteria.noiLienTucDu: Speaks continuously and at enough length for Part 2; uses natural spoken connectors: actually, Basically, First and foremost, Honestly speaking.
write.criteria.tuVungTheoChu: A good range of topic vocabulary: noise-cancelling headphones, indispensable gadget, background distractions, personal quiet bubble.
write.criteria.kiemSoatTotCau: Good control of complex sentences with relative clauses (which have genuinely become…) and participle clauses; the range of structures is still somewhat limited.
write.criteria.banChepKhongThe2: A transcript cannot show pronunciation; at this level the listener generally understands easily, though stress and intonation are not fully consistent.
write.criteria.traLoiDaiMach: A long, coherent answer that covers every point on the cue card; ideas connect naturally, with little reliance on connectives.
write.criteria.tuItThongDung2: Less common words used precisely: sheer frustration, tactile sensation, strikes an exquisite balance.
write.criteria.cauTrucPhucDa2: A wide range of complex structures: conditionals (If I had to single out…), noun clauses (What sets this device apart…), participle clauses (shielding me from…); almost no errors.
write.criteria.banChepKhongThe3: A transcript cannot show pronunciation; at band 8 the speaker is easily understood throughout, with flexible rhythm and intonation.
write.criteria.speakingTuBand5: Speaking from band 5.0 to 6.5: longer, smoother answers
write.criteria.speakingTuBand6: Speaking from band 6.5 to 8.0: flexible and precise
write.criteria.gopCauDonNgan: Combine short simple sentences into complex ones with subordinating conjunctions (although, because, whereas) or relative clauses (which, who).
write.criteria.boThoiQuenMo: Stop starting every sentence with Firstly, Secondly or In my opinion; use more natural openers: One notable factor is that…, A further consideration is…
write.criteria.hocTuTheoCum: Learn words in collocations: instead of just "pollution", learn "tackle air pollution" and "reduce carbon emissions".
write.criteria.trienKhaiMoiY: Develop each idea with P-E-E: Point → Explanation → Example.
write.criteria.dungNgonNguRao: Use hedging when you generalise: tends to, is likely to, There is a risk that… instead of absolute claims.
write.criteria.lienKetBangTham: Link ideas through reference rather than sentence-initial connectors: This trend, Such measures, These consequences.
write.criteria.boCacCauSao: Drop worn-out clichés: every coin has two sides, a double-edged sword, in a nutshell.
write.criteria.moRongYDen: Extend ideas fully: give causes, consequences and limits of each point, with a specific example.

write.criteria.dungTuNoiVan: Use natural spoken connectors: To be honest, As a matter of fact, Speaking of…, not just and, because, so.
write.criteria.suaAmCuoiS: Fix final sounds /s/, /z/, /t/, /d/: a common error that makes words hard to recognise.
write.criteria.luyen15PhutMoi: Practise 15 minutes a day: shadow a model recording, then record yourself and listen back.
write.criteria.luyenTrongAmCau: Work on sentence stress and intonation: stress the content words and let your voice fall at the end of statements.
write.criteria.khongCanTuDao: You do not need "big words": high scores come from less common words, idioms and phrasal verbs used in the right context.
write.criteria.tuSuaNheNhang: Self-correct smoothly when you slip: "Or rather…", "What I mean is…", then carry on.
write.criteria.part3MoRong: Part 3: extend answers with reasons, examples and comparisons, and look at several angles (personal, social, generational).

learn.method.moiNgayNenHoc: How many new words should I learn each day?
learn.method.1020TuLa: 10–20 is reasonable. Each new word generates about 5–8 reviews in the first month, so learning too many will pile up your reviews. Adjust new words per day and the review session limit in Settings.
learn.method.quenKhongNhoRa: “Again” = you couldn’t recall it → the card goes back to the learning step (1 min) and its stability drops. “Hard” = you recalled it with effort → the interval grows only a little. Answer honestly – FSRS uses this to build the best schedule for you.
learn.method.mucTieuGhiNho: What does a 90% retention target mean?
learn.method.khiMotTuDen: When a word comes up for review, you have a ~90% chance of remembering it. Raising it to 95% makes memory stronger but nearly doubles your reviews; lowering it to 85% means fewer reviews. 90% is the recommended balance.
learn.method.boLoVaiNgay: What if I miss a few days?
learn.method.khongSaoFsrsTinh: No problem – FSRS accounts for the actual time that has passed. Words you still remember after a long gap get spaced out further; review your “Fading” words first and cap your session so you don’t get overwhelmed.
learn.method.viSaoNenLuu: Why save words with their original sentences?
learn.method.cauGocChoBiet: The original sentence shows real usage: which prepositions and collocations the word takes and what nuance it carries. Seeing the context again when you review helps you use the word correctly in speaking and writing – exactly what IELTS Lexical Resource assesses.
learn.fix.tuNayVietSai: This word is misspelled. Learn the correct spelling – words you misspell often are added to your review cards.
learn.fix.daiTuIToi: The pronoun “I” is always written as a capital letter, wherever it appears in the sentence.
learn.fix.dungAnTruocTu: Use “an” before a VOWEL SOUND (an apple, an hour – silent h) and “a” before a CONSONANT SOUND (a book, a university /juː/, a one-day trip). It depends on the sound, not the letter.
learn.fix.tuNayBiGo: This word is typed twice in a row. Delete one of them.
learn.fix.chuNguVaDong: The subject and verb do not agree: he/she/it and singular nouns take a verb with -s/-es (has, does, is, was); I/you/we/they and plural nouns take the base form (have, do, are, were).
learn.fix.everyoneSomebodyNobodyEach: Everyone, somebody, nobody, each… are SINGULAR subjects, so the verb is singular: everyone is, each has.
learn.fix.sauCanCouldShould: After can/could/should/must/may/might/will/would, use the base verb WITHOUT “to”: You should study (not should to study).
learn.fix.couldVeShouldVe: “could’ve / should’ve” sounds like “of”, but it is written HAVE: could have + past participle (could have done).
learn.fix.thiHoanThanhDung: Perfect tenses use have/has/had + the PAST PARTICIPLE, not the past simple form: have gone, has eaten, had written.
learn.fix.sauDoDoesDid: After do/does/did (in negatives and questions too) the main verb stays in the BASE FORM: didn’t go, does she like (not didn’t went, does she likes).
learn.fix.makeLetTanNgu: make/let + object + base verb WITHOUT “to”: It made me laugh, Let him go.
learn.fix.motSoDongTu: Some verbs are always followed by the -ING form, not “to + verb”: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, consider, keep, practise, miss, risk, suggest… → I enjoy reading.
learn.fix.trongLookForwardTo: In “look forward to”, “to” is a PREPOSITION, so it is followed by an -ING form or a noun: I look forward to hearing from you.
learn.fix.agreeDisagreeLaDong: “Agree / disagree” are VERBS, so do not use them with am/is/are: I agree (not I am agree).
learn.fix.trongMenhDeIf: In an if/when/unless clause about the future, use the PRESENT SIMPLE, not will: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.
learn.fix.danhTuKhongDem2: UNCOUNTABLE nouns (information, advice, equipment, furniture, knowledge, evidence, homework, luggage, feedback) have no plural -s. Use “a piece of / some / much”.
learn.fix.tinhTuNganDa: Short adjectives that already end in -er/-est (better, bigger, easiest) do NOT take more/most: better (not more better).
learn.fix.soSanhHonDung: Comparatives use THAN (bigger than). “Then” means “after that / at that time”.
learn.fix.forKhoangThoiGian: FOR + a period of time (for three years), SINCE + a point in time (since 2020, since Monday).
learn.fix.motSoDongTu2: Some verbs and adjectives take a fixed preposition – or NO preposition at all. Learn the whole phrase: discuss something, depend on, interested in, on the other hand.
learn.fix.cumCoDinhLa: The fixed phrase is ON the other hand, not “in the other hand”.
learn.fix.despiteKhongCoOf: DESPITE has no “of” (despite the rain), but IN SPITE OF does.
learn.fix.tiengVietNoiMac: Many languages say “Although…, but…”, but English uses only ONE conjunction: Although it rained, we went out (remove “but”).
learn.fix.tiengVietNoiVi: Many languages say “Because…, so…”, but English uses only ONE conjunction: Because it was late, we left (remove “so”).
learn.fix.explainDescribeSuggestSth: Explain / describe / suggest + something + TO + a person: Please explain it to me (not explain me).
learn.fix.yourCuaBanYour: YOUR shows possession (your book); YOU’RE = you are (you’re welcome, you’re right).
learn.fix.itSItIs: IT’S = it is / it has (it’s important); ITS shows possession (its tail) – no apostrophe.
learn.fix.theirCuaHoTheir: THEIR shows possession (their house), THERE = in that place / there is, THEY’RE = they are.
learn.fix.quyTacTrinhBay: English layout rules: no space BEFORE a comma, full stop, question mark or exclamation mark, one space AFTER it, and a capital letter at the start of a sentence.
learn.fix.tuCumNoiDung: A linking word or phrase at the START of a sentence (However, Moreover, In conclusion, For example…) is followed by a comma.
learn.fix.cumNayLapY: This phrase repeats an idea (return already means “go back”; in my opinion = I think). Keep it short to sound more professional.
learn.fix.cauDungNhungTu: The sentence is correct, but this word is rather general. A more precise word sounds more natural and scores higher for vocabulary (IELTS Lexical Resource). Choose the one that fits the context.
